newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian traders dismiss TOCOM's Brent futures plan.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders dismiss TOCOM's Brent futures plan.

text.p: The Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) has added its name to that of other markets planning to trade North Sea Brent crude futures in Asia -- but traders forecast few users.
"I'm afraid not many people are going to use it," one Japanese trader said.

The giant New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) and International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) in London, currently the home of Brent futures, two weeks ago announced plans to trade Brent on an electronic trading system.
The Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) already lists Brent and says it has exclusive rights to do so from 0100 GMT to 1000 GMT.
TOCOM's Mitsuhiro Onosato, general manager of planning, revealed in an interview with Reuters this week the exchange was considering listing a Brent contract in the fiscal year beginning April 1999.
He said TOCOM planned to work out ways to list the contract without infringing on SIMEX agreements concerning Brent.

But the Petroleum Association of Japan, an industry group comprising oil refiners and wholesalers, has said interest to trade futures among Japan's energy firms would not be enough to support a market.

An official at the Ministry of International Trade and Industry's (MITI) agency of natural resources and energy, which supervises the energy industry, said oil futures should be listed only if the oil industry supported the idea.
Energy brokers and traders said on Thursday there was little interest in all of Asia to trade Brent futures -- considered the world's most international crude oil.
"Trading volume in Singapore would have been much higher if we really needed the Brent contract in this region," the Japanese trader said.
The contract on SIMEX has been dogged with poor trading volumes since it was first listed in 1995, trading a few hundred lots per day compared with 40,000 to 60,000 on the IPE.
"TOCOM would face the same fundamental problem that any other exchange in Asia would face," said an energy broker in Singapore.
"Most physical crude is traded in London time, so that is the time crude is hedged. We are totally trading out of London's pockets all the time," he said.
Brokers said until Asian crude buyers start concluding more deals during Asia hours, Brent futures would fail to gain support in the region.
TOCOM's Onosato was unworried by the task ahead.
"When we tried to list gold futures in the early 1980s, traders almost unanimously said it was bound to fail," he said. "Today, Tokyo's trading volume is the world's second-largest only after COMEX."
He also said physical trading would pick up during the Asian trading day once Tokyo's Brent futures gain enough liquidity.

"Some say physical trading has to be active for successful futures. Others say liquid futures markets are necessary for brisk spot trading," he said. "It's like a chicken-and-egg discussion. But we have to start from somewhere."
